newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French Cap Gemini happy to part with Daimler.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French Cap Gemini happy to part with Daimler.

text.p: French computer services group Cap Gemini said on Thursday it was happy German industrial giant Daimler-Benz was ending their alliance after six years as its biggest shareholder.
Daimler's announcement that it would sell its 24.4 percent stake in Cap Gemini knocked several percent off the French firm's share price by killing any prospect of a full takeover.

French holding company CGIP, which already has 20 percent of Cap Gemini, said it would decide within a month whether to buy Daimler's stake and said the German firm's move had ended "a long period of uncertainty".

Cap Gemini put a positive spin on the news, saying the relationship had floundered because of deep-rooted differences on strategy and management culture, and that it would now be free to expand through acquisitions, notably in the United States.
"I am glad that the right decision has been taken. We're now taking our freedom in all our markets," Cap Gemini chief executive Serge Kampf said.
"We will be able to pursue new geographical developments and go ahead with acquisitions, notably in the United States," Kampf told afternoon daily Le Monde in an interview.
The link up in Germany with the creation of the Debis joint venture at the start of the 1990s had been a "real test of our ability to work together".
"The result was that we ended up excluded from the German market."

"Debis started to compete with us on our European markets, seeking last year to buy French firm GSI. We opposed this vehemently. Now Debis is a suitor to buy dutch firm Rocade. We are equally opposed," he said.

"The partnership over six years with Debis Systemhaus has not been as fruitful as we had hoped. Cultures and management methods are very different. Debis is much more geared towards heavy computer services while we are closer to the consultancy domain," he said.
Kampf said his company had not been in favour of Daimler taking control of the firm because the move would have obliged Cap Gemini to unwind its U.S. business.
U.S. law did not allow industrial or services activity to be bank-controlled and Daimler's main shareholder is Deutsche Bank, he said.
"Our presence in the United States is of capital importance to us. Among the top 10 computer services firms in the world nine are American. The only exception is Cap Gemini, ranked fifth," he said.
Kampf also said he expected Cap Gemini to make a net profit of over 500 million francs ($85.9 million) this year and that he expected a profit of 700-800 million francs in 1998.
"We've got out of our troubles of the past," he said. "Our net result should exceed 500 million francs this year and come in around 700-800 million francs next year," he said.

Daimler said on Wednesday it plans to withdraw from Cap Gemini "in the medium term" and its Debis unit said on Thursday it planned to recover an entire 1.3 billion marks investment which it had made in the French firm.
Kampf said Cap Gemini had been left in the dark on Daimler's intentions since an option to buy out the firm expired in 1996 and that the announcement on Wednesday came as a relief.
Cap Gemini made a net attributable profit of 280 million francs in 1996, versus 52 million the year before.
Cap Gemini shares lost more than five percent at one stage and stood 4.64 percent down at 329.0 francs at 1315 GMT, when the CAC-40 blue-chip index was 0.22 percent higher.
